html:
Maya script was the writing system of the Maya, in use from at least the 3rd century BCE until the Spanish conquest in the 1500s and 1600s. It is the only writing system of the ancient Americas that can be read in full today.

It mixes two kinds of signs, much like Japanese: logograms that stand for whole words, and about two hundred syllable signs that spell sounds. A scribe could write a word either way, or both at once. The earliest known texts come from sites such as San Bartolo in Guatemala.

The Maya wrote on stone monuments, stairways, pottery and bark-paper books. Most texts record kings: births, accessions, wars, captures and rituals, each dated in the Long Count calendar. Writing was a skill of the elite. Spanish friars burned most of the books, and only four survived.

For a long time scholars could read the numbers and dates but not the words, and many believed the script was not linked to speech. That changed from the 1950s, when the Soviet scholar Yuri Knorozov showed the signs worked as syllables. In the 1970s and 1980s readers like Linda Schele and David Stuart opened up the dynastic history of whole cities. It ranks with the decipherment of Egyptian hieroglyphs and cuneiform as one of the great feats of reading the past.
sum: Maya script was the writing system of the Maya, in use from at least the 3rd century BCE until the Spanish conquest in the 1500s and 1600s. It is the only writing system of the ancient Americas that can be read in full today.
